r: Introduction to Construction Project Management teaches the project life-cycle — programming, design, construction, operations, decommissioning — as a conceptual framework for the built environment. The applied tasks are managerial and analytical: framing project phases, coordinating stakeholders, and organizing life-cycle information, activities mapped to O*NET's coordinating, planning, and information-processing categories. Observed-usage data shows management and office tasks are a large and rising share of AI use, so a model can already draft phase plans and summarize life-cycle concepts. The binding constraint here is not embodiment but the course's foundational role: it is the introductory substrate the CPM major builds on, and the deterministic rule caps an intro-scaffolding course at Medium. At 24 months, near-zero curricular restructuring and modest diffusion (Census data put firm adoption near a fifth) keep realized substitution partial. Rating Medium — the management-knowledge is exposed, but the foundational function holds it below full erosion.

By 2031, AI will competently generate the life-cycle planning artifacts this course's knowledge produces — phase schedules, programming summaries, coordination documents — as task-exposure research places office and management writing among positively-exposed activities. The instrumental case for learning to assemble these frameworks by hand erodes: the model does the drafting and organizing, and the student's role shifts toward specifying and reviewing. What survives is the conceptual grounding that lets a manager judge whether an AI-generated life-cycle plan is coherent, plus the course's status as the introductory substrate for the CPM major. That foundational-scaffolding function caps the rating at Medium rather than letting it rise to High. The hedge is genuine: how much an introductory survey needs to teach when AI fluently produces its outputs is a pedagogical question, not a settled one. Rating Medium, held there by the course's load-bearing role in the degree sequence.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most life-cycle planning and coordination knowledge-work, with construction managers concentrated in judgment, negotiation, and oversight. The instrumental rationale for teaching students to produce phase frameworks themselves is substantially eroded, and F1 rises accordingly. Yet this remains the foundational introduction the rest of the major depends on: students cannot meaningfully supervise AI-generated project plans without the life-cycle vocabulary and structure the course installs, so the deterministic rule holds it at Medium rather than High. Ten-year forecasting is inherently wide, and construction's fragmented, physically-anchored delivery may slow diffusion below the capability frontier — METR's fast capability-doubling trend describes what models can do, not what jobsites adopt. The honest read is that the course's outputs automate while its scaffolding purpose persists. Rating Medium, capped by foundational role, with the residual value shifting toward interpreting and validating machine-produced plans.
CPM 1010.d: Students will study the project life-cycle concepts in construction project management. This life-cycle concept includes the built environment from programming and design to operations and decommissioning.

r: Introduction to Facilities Management teaches FM concepts and a leader's role in tactical planning — scheduling and accomplishing the daily tasks that keep an organization's facilities operating. The applied work is administrative and analytical: work-order planning, resource scheduling, and operational coordination, mapping to O*NET's scheduling-work, organizing, and administrative-support activities. These are precisely the office-and-management tasks observed-usage data shows as a large, growing share of model use, and a model already drafts maintenance schedules and tactical plans competently. The course carries no licensure lock and no embodiment barrier — the binding constraint is simply how exposed this planning knowledge is. At 24 months, though, near-zero curricular change and uneven diffusion (Census figures put firm AI adoption around a fifth) keep realized substitution partial, and the course's contributory role in the FM concentration provides a mild floor. Rating Medium: exposed knowledge-work, not yet fully displaced in the near term.

By 2031, AI will handle the bulk of tactical FM planning — generating and optimizing daily schedules, allocating resources, and drafting operational documentation — the applied tasks this course's knowledge serves. Task-exposure research classifies administrative scheduling and management writing as highly exposed, and enterprise deployment skews heavily toward automation of such office work. With no embodiment, no licensure mandate, and only a weak contributory role in the major, little caps the rating: the FM-planning competence the course teaches is broadly automatable. The residual is supervisory judgment — deciding which AI-generated schedule fits an organization's constraints — but that is a fraction of the introductory content. The rating rises to High. The hedge is that facilities operations remain physically anchored and adoption in mid-sized organizations may lag capability, so realized substitution could trail the frontier. Still, the direction is clear: the knowledge-work core of this course is squarely exposed.

A decade out, AI is deeply embedded in facilities operations — predictive maintenance analytics, autonomous scheduling, energy and space optimization — performing most of the tactical planning knowledge-work this course teaches. The instrumental case for a student learning to plan and schedule FM tasks by hand is substantially eroded, with human managers focused on contracting, judgment, and accountability. Nothing structural holds the rating down: no clinical embodiment, no board-approved curriculum, no foundational-scaffolding cap. Rating High. The ten-year band is wide, and I hedge on diffusion specifically — buildings are physical, vendor ecosystems fragmented, and Acemoglu's modest macro-productivity estimate cautions that economy-wide automation arrives slower than raw capability implies. The competence most likely to persist is oversight of automated facility systems, which this introductory course only partly builds. The honest framing: the applied planning tasks automate substantially, and the course's instrumental necessity erodes markedly even as physical FM work continues.
CPM 1100.d: In this course students are introduced to the basic concepts that describe the field of facility management and how it can be of value to an organization. In this course students review a leader's role in tactical planning for how to schedule and accomplish daily facility management tasks that support the operation of an organization's facilities.

r: Engineering Principles for Construction Managers builds a foundational understanding of structural behavior and building systems (mechanical, electrical, piping), engineering fundamentals, building codes, and system integration so managers can collaborate with engineers. The applied tasks — engineering calculation, code interpretation, and reasoning about how systems behave — map to O*NET's analyzing-data and evaluating-information activities. Some of this is exposed: task-exposure research shows quantitative problem-solving is automatable, and models solve textbook structural and MEP problems. But two constraints bind. Verifying an AI's structural or code claim genuinely requires the knowledge, because a confident wrong answer about a load path or code provision is dangerous and its failure non-obvious — the jagged-frontier evidence, where users outside the frontier were markedly less accurate, is directly relevant. And the course is foundational scaffolding for the major. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire this engineering literacy is not eroded. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will fluently perform the engineering calculations and code look-ups this course covers and will explain structural and MEP behavior on demand, weakening the rationale for students to work problems by hand. Yet the competence the course actually builds — enough engineering judgment to recognize when a generated answer is wrong before it reaches a jobsite — grows more valuable, not less. Structural and code errors carry safety and liability consequences and fail non-obviously, so the verification burden keeps a knowledgeable human necessary; the dampener in the rule reflects exactly this. As foundational scaffolding for the construction-management sequence, the course's place is also capped from eroding. The rating stays Low. The hedge: as models become more reliable on routine engineering questions, the share of the course that is pure execution shrinks toward pure verification — a real shift in emphasis, but not a removal of the instrumental need.

A decade out, AI will handle most routine structural and MEP analysis and code checking, and much of the calculation this course teaches will be automated. The execution rationale is largely gone. But the human ability to verify that an AI-proposed structural approach is safe and code-compliant remains a necessary competence in a domain where errors injure people, and this foundational course is where construction managers first acquire it. The deterministic rule lifts the rating to Medium at this horizon — the applied tasks are substantially automatable — while verification burden and foundational role keep it from High. Ten-year uncertainty is wide, and I hedge on how much residual engineering-verification work managers retain versus delegating to licensed engineers and their tools. The direction is clear: engineering computation automates, but the judgment to catch a dangerous machine error persists, and this course installs its groundwork. Rating Medium.
CPM 2000.d: Construction project management students gain a foundational understanding of structural behavior and building systems, including mechanical, electrical, and piping (MEP). Students explore fundamental engineering principles, building codes, and system integration, gaining the applied knowledge needed for effective collaboration with engineers and preparation for industry careers.

r: Building Technology and Software introduces applying technology to facilities and built environments, how information technology and AI link to modern building design, and how to choose and implement technological solutions against building needs. The applied work is technology evaluation and selection — assessing tools, matching capabilities to requirements, and planning implementations — mapping to O*NET's evaluating-information and making-decisions activities. This is digital knowledge-work with no embodiment barrier, and observed-usage data places software and information tasks (Computer and Mathematical) as the single largest category of model use, so AI already assists technology comparison and selection reasoning. There is no licensure lock. At 24 months, the constraint is only diffusion and the course's modest role in the FM concentration: near-zero curricular change and roughly one-fifth firm adoption keep realized substitution partial. Rating Medium — the tech-selection knowledge is highly exposed, but near-term erosion is incomplete.

By 2031, AI will competently perform the technology-evaluation and implementation-planning tasks this course teaches — surveying building-technology options, matching solutions to needs, and drafting adoption plans — work squarely in the Computer-and-Mathematical usage category that observed data shows models handle most. With no embodiment, no institutional mandate, and only a weak place in the major, little caps the rating. There is a self-referential irony: a course teaching how to choose AI and IT solutions for buildings is itself highly exposed to AI performing that selection analysis. The residual is judgment about organizational fit and integration risk, narrower than the course's content. The rating rises to High. The hedge is verification-flavored — the jagged-frontier evidence warns that AI technology recommendations can be confidently wrong, so a knowledgeable human check retains value — but that is a thin protection relative to how automatable the core selection work is.

A decade out, AI will routinely evaluate building-technology options and design implementation strategies, and the knowledge-work this course teaches is largely performed by machines. The instrumental case for learning technology-selection reasoning by hand is substantially eroded, with practitioners concentrated in integration judgment and vendor accountability. No structural constraint holds the rating down — no embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding cap. Rating High. The ten-year band is genuinely wide; I hedge on diffusion, since building-technology ecosystems are fragmented and capital-intensive and Census/Acemoglu evidence shows adoption and productivity gains arriving slower than capability. The most durable residue is oversight — knowing when an AI-recommended building system is inappropriate — which this introductory course only begins to build. The honest read: a course about applying technology and AI to buildings sees its own applied tasks automated, and its instrumental necessity erodes markedly, even as humans remain accountable for the choices.
CPM 2010.d: In this course, students are introduced to the application of technology to various types of facilities and built environments. Students learn how information technology and artificial intelligence are linked to modern building design and how to better choose and implement technological solutions with building needs in mind.

r: Blueprint Reading and Interpretation develops skill in reading construction drawings — architectural, structural, civil, and MEP — including notation, standards, and conventions, using digital tools to navigate and review plans. The applied task is visual-technical interpretation of drawings, mapping to O*NET's getting-information and inspecting-documents activities. Multimodal AI is improving at parsing drawings, giving real exposure, but reliable plan interpretation is not yet deployed at scale, and misreading a drawing produces costly, downstream, non-obvious errors, so verification requires the skill itself — the dampener applies. The course is also explicit foundational scaffolding: it 'prepares students for advanced coursework in estimating, scheduling, and project management' and is prerequisite to several upper courses, which caps the rating at Medium under the rule. At 24 months, with modest multimodal reliability and near-zero curricular change, the instrumental need to read drawings competently is not eroded. Rating Low.

By 2031, multimodal models will read and cross-reference construction drawings far more reliably, extracting quantities, flagging conflicts, and summarizing plan content — automating much of the interpretation this course teaches. The instrumental case shifts from reading drawings by hand toward directing and checking AI plan-review, and the distinctive residue is verification: a plausible-but-wrong extraction from a drawing propagates into estimates and schedules, so the trained reader who catches it remains necessary, echoing the jagged-frontier caution. Foundational scaffolding caps the rating at Medium — estimating, scheduling, and PM coursework depend on this drawing literacy — and prevents a rise to High. The rating moves to Medium. The hedge is real: how reliably models interpret dense, non-standardized construction documents by 2031 is uncertain, and if reliability lags, more of the human reading role persists. Either way the competence becomes more oversight than production.

A decade out, AI will interpret construction drawings competently as a matter of course, extracting and reconciling architectural, structural, and MEP information automatically, and the manual reading rationale is largely eroded. But the ability to verify that a machine has read a drawing correctly — before the error reaches procurement or the field — remains a necessary human competence, and this course is where that literacy is founded, scaffolding the estimating and scheduling sequence. The deterministic rule holds the rating at Medium, capped by foundational role from reaching High. Ten-year uncertainty is wide; I hedge on both model reliability on messy real-world document sets and on construction's slow diffusion. The direction is clear: drawing interpretation automates substantially, yet the verification competence and the course's substrate function persist. Rating Medium, with the residual value concentrated in catching the non-obvious misread that automated plan review would otherwise pass downstream.
CPM 2100.d: Introduction to reading and interpreting construction drawings with an emphasis on architectural, structural, civil, and MEP systems. Students develop skills in drawing notation, standards, and conventions while using digital tools to navigate and review plans. Prepares students for advanced coursework in estimating, scheduling, and project management.

r: Surveying for Construction Project Management covers distance, elevation, and angle measurement; the trigonometry behind it; traverse computations, error theory, and coordinate geometry for construction layout and mapmaking; with applied demonstrations using surveying instruments, CAD/data collectors, and field-style exercises. Two layers coexist: the computation (trig, traverse, coordinate geometry) is highly exposed — task-exposure research places quantitative work as automatable — but the field operation of instruments and physical site layout is embodied, real-time, and low-exposure, the category observed-usage data shows least represented. Layout errors are expensive and compound, so verification also requires the knowledge. The embodiment of the instrument-and-field work is the binding constraint, triggering the dampener. At 24 months, robotic total stations and GPS exist but the course's field-judgment competence is not displaced, and no curricular change intervenes. Rating Low — the math is exposed, the fieldwork is not.

By 2031, surveying automation — robotic total stations, GNSS, drone photogrammetry, and AI processing of point clouds — will absorb much of the computation and even routine data capture this course teaches, and the traverse-and-coordinate math is fully automatable. Yet the embodied core persists: setting out a real site, operating instruments under field conditions, and exercising the judgment to trust or reject a measurement remain in-person, low-exposure activities that automation augments rather than performs. Verification compounds the protection — a layout error carries real cost and its failure is non-obvious. The dampener keeps the rating Low across this horizon. The hedge is that automated survey workflows may deskill parts of the field task, shifting the competence toward equipment oversight; but the physical, real-time act of construction layout, and the judgment to catch a bad fix, keep the instrumental need intact through five years. Rating Low.

A decade out, survey data capture and processing will be substantially automated — autonomous instruments, drone-based site scanning, and AI point-cloud interpretation handling most routine layout and mapping. The computational and even some field-capture rationale erodes, and F1 rises. But construction layout remains a physical, real-time task performed on uneven, changing sites, and the judgment to verify that an automated fix is correct before crews build to it stays a human competence; embodiment does not vanish by 2036. The deterministic rule lifts the rating only to Medium, held down by the field-and-verification core. Ten-year uncertainty is wide; I hedge on how much site layout genuinely autonomizes versus remaining human-supervised. The honest read: the surveying mathematics automates fully and field capture largely, but the embodied, error-critical act of construction layout resists direct substitution, so the course's instrumental necessity erodes only partway. Rating Medium.
CPM 2200.d: This course is an introduction to the principles of surveying for construction, including measurement of distances, elevations, and angles. Students review the essential trigonometry required for surveying applications, then apply it to traverse computations, error theory, and coordinate geometry to support construction layout and mapmaking. Applied demonstrations with surveying instruments, CAD/data collectors, and field-style exercises emphasize the accuracy and role of surveying data in engineering design and construction project management.

r: Career Preparedness helps students prepare for internships and careers by refining resumes, practicing interview techniques, building networking confidence, and learning employer expectations, workplace professionalism, and organizational culture. The tasks split: resume and cover-letter drafting is highly exposed — writing is among the most positively-associated activities in task-exposure research, and models produce competent application materials instantly — but the graded core is interpersonal and embodied: live interviewing, real-time networking, and enacting professional presence. These map to O*NET's communicating, establishing-relationships, and performing-for/interacting activities, which observed-usage data shows least automated. Embodiment of the interpersonal practice is the binding constraint, triggering the dampener. At 24 months, AI writes the resume but cannot develop the student's capacity to interview and network in person, and no institutional change alters that. Rating Low — the document tasks are exposed, the interpersonal competence the course actually builds is not.

By 2031, AI will draft and even rehearse-coach application materials and simulate interview questions, fully automating the preparation-document stage this course touches. But the competence that matters — presence, rapport, and real-time responsiveness in interviews and professional networking — is embodied and interpersonal, sitting squarely in the low-exposure categories that task-exposure research and observed usage both flag as resistant. The dampener holds the rating Low. The hedge is modest: as virtual interviews and AI-mediated hiring spread, some networking migrates to digital channels a model can assist with, and the balance of the course could tilt toward navigating AI-screened hiring. Yet the instrumental need to develop human professional presence does not erode — it is the point of the course, and automation cannot perform it on the student's behalf. Rating Low, protected by the embodied, real-time interpersonal nature of career readiness.

A decade out, AI will handle essentially all application-document production and much interview preparation, and hiring pipelines will be heavily AI-mediated. Even so, the embodied competence this course builds — interviewing, networking, and enacting professional judgment in real time with other people — is not a task AI performs for the student, and it remains among the least-exposed activities in the evidence base. The dampener keeps the rating Low through 2036. Ten-year uncertainty is real, but it concerns how hiring and networking are conducted under ubiquitous AI, not whether a student still needs the human interpersonal capacity the course develops. The plausible shift is in what candidates must know about AI-driven hiring, not in the necessity of the presence-based skills themselves. Rating Low with reasonable confidence — the document tasks fully automate, yet the course's interpersonal core is definitionally embodied and resists substitution across the full horizon.
CPM 2950.d: In this course, construction project management students prepare for internships and careers by developing essential professional skills. Students refine resumes, practice interview techniques, and build networking confidence while exploring employer expectations, workplace professionalism, and organizational culture with an emphasis on inclusion and communication.

r: Workplace Safety prepares students to work safely in construction environments and to supervise others on safety, emphasizing practical hazard-specific content, and it delivers OSHA 30 training with DOL course-completion certification. The applied work is jobsite hazard recognition and real-time safety supervision — embodied, in-person activities mapping to O*NET's inspecting-equipment/structures and monitoring activities that observed-usage data shows least automated. AI can draft safety plans and surface hazard information, giving partial exposure, but recognizing and responding to hazards on an active site is physical and real-time, and the error cost is fatal and non-obvious, so verification demands a knowledgeable human — both dampeners apply. The OSHA 30/DOL certification adds an institutional credential the course confers. At 24 months, the instrumental need to develop embodied safety competence is untouched by capability. Rating Low, protected by embodiment, extreme verification burden, and the certification's role.

By 2031, AI will assist safety management substantially — generating job-hazard analyses, monitoring site imagery for violations, and drafting compliance documentation — augmenting but not replacing the on-site supervisor. The competence the course builds is embodied jobsite hazard recognition and the real-time judgment to intervene, low-exposure work that automation supports rather than performs, and the verification burden is definitional: a missed hazard kills, and the failure mode is non-obvious, so a trained human must remain in the loop. The dampeners hold the rating Low. The OSHA 30/DOL certification and the course's role feeding the capstone add further inertia. The hedge is that computer-vision safety monitoring may take over more routine surveillance by 2031, shifting the supervisor toward exception-handling; but the embodied, life-safety-critical core keeps the instrumental need intact. Rating Low — capability grows as a tool, not a substitute, in a domain where errors are fatal.

A decade out, AI-driven safety monitoring — persistent computer vision, wearables, predictive hazard analytics — will absorb much routine surveillance and documentation. But construction sites remain physical and hazardous, and the embodied competence to recognize and respond to danger in real time, and to verify that an automated system has not missed something lethal, resists substitution; the error cost keeps a knowledgeable human necessary. The deterministic rule lifts the rating only to Medium, held down by embodiment and verification even as documentation and monitoring automate. Ten-year uncertainty is wide, and I hedge on how much on-site supervision genuinely autonomizes versus staying human-led for liability and life-safety reasons. The OSHA/DOL certification framework also shows no near-term path to removal. The honest read: safety analytics automate, yet the physical, fatal-consequence core of jobsite safety supervision endures, so instrumental necessity erodes only partway. Rating Medium.
CPM 3000.d: Students in this course prepare to work safely in construction environments and allow the informed supervision of other workers regarding workplace safety. Emphasis is placed on practical applications of safety theory and hazard specific content. The course also provides Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) 30 training and Department of Labor (DOL) course completion certification for students taking the course.

r: Facilities Maintenance and Operations introduces the operations, maintenance, and energy-management requirements of various facilities and built environments. The applied work is knowledge-based planning and analysis — maintenance program design, operational scheduling, and energy performance evaluation — mapping to O*NET's scheduling, analyzing-data, and evaluating-information activities. This is administrative and analytical knowledge-work; observed-usage data shows management and office tasks are a large, rising share of model use, and AI already drafts maintenance plans and analyzes energy data. There is no licensure lock and no embodiment barrier at the course level, since it teaches the requirements of O&M rather than performing physical maintenance — so the binding constraint is how exposed this management knowledge is. At 24 months, near-zero curricular change and roughly one-fifth firm adoption (per Census data) keep realized substitution partial. Rating Medium — exposed operations-management knowledge, not yet fully displaced near-term.

By 2031, AI will perform much of the O&M knowledge-work this course teaches — generating and optimizing maintenance schedules, running energy analytics, and drafting operational documentation — the applied tasks its knowledge serves. Task-exposure research places administrative and analytical management activities among exposed categories, and enterprise deployment skews toward automating such office work. With no embodiment barrier in the course content, no licensure mandate, and a terminal elective role, little caps the rating: operations-and-energy-management planning is broadly automatable. The residual is judgment about physical-system constraints and vendor coordination, narrower than the course's content. The rating rises to High. The hedge is that facilities are physical and maintenance execution stays embodied, so mid-sized-organization adoption may trail capability, keeping realized substitution below the frontier. Still, the knowledge-work this course actually teaches — the planning and analysis, not the wrench-turning — sits squarely in the exposed categories, and its instrumental necessity erodes materially.

A decade out, AI will handle most facilities operations planning and energy management — autonomous scheduling, predictive maintenance analytics, continuous energy optimization — performing the knowledge-work this course teaches. The instrumental case for learning to design O&M programs by hand is substantially eroded, with humans focused on contracting, capital decisions, and accountability. No structural constraint holds the rating down: the course teaches management knowledge, not embodied maintenance, so no clinical embodiment or foundational cap applies. Rating High. The ten-year band is wide; I hedge on diffusion, since building systems are capital-intensive and fragmented and Acemoglu's modest productivity estimate warns that economy-wide automation lags capability. The durable residue is oversight of automated facility systems, which this course only partly builds. The honest framing: the O&M planning and analysis tasks automate substantially, and the course's instrumental necessity erodes markedly, even as physical maintenance labor continues on the ground.
CPM 3020.d: In this course, students are introduced to operations, maintenance, and energy management requirements of various types of facilities and built environments.

r: Soils and Concrete in Construction covers classification, testing, mix design, placement, and quality control of soils and concrete, emphasizing practical applications for site evaluation, safety, and construction practices. The applied work is materials testing and field quality control — sampling, running tests, evaluating placement, and judging conformance — mapping to O*NET's inspecting, testing, and handling-materials activities that observed-usage data shows least automated. Mix-design computation is exposed, but the hands-on testing and on-site QC are embodied and real-time, and materials failures carry structural and safety consequences that are costly and non-obvious, so verification requires the knowledge — both dampeners apply. Embodiment of the testing-and-QC work is the binding constraint. At 24 months, AI can compute a mix design, but it cannot sample soil, cast cylinders, or judge a pour on site, and no curricular change intervenes. Rating Low — the calculation is exposed, the embodied materials work is not.

By 2031, AI will handle mix-design optimization, test-data interpretation, and QC documentation, and sensor-instrumented testing may automate more measurement — eroding the computational rationale. But the embodied core persists: physically sampling and testing materials, observing placement, and exercising the field judgment to accept or reject work remain in-person, low-exposure tasks, and the verification burden is severe because a bad pour or misclassified soil fails structurally and non-obviously. The dampeners hold the rating Low. The hedge is that automated materials testing and embedded sensors could absorb more routine measurement by 2031, shifting the competence toward interpreting instrument output; but the physical testing-and-QC act, and the judgment to catch a dangerous materials failure, keep the instrumental need intact. Rating Low — capability enters as an analytical aid in a domain where the safety-critical work is done with one's hands on the material and on the site.

A decade out, materials testing and QC will be substantially instrumented — automated labs, embedded sensors, AI interpretation of test streams — absorbing much routine measurement and the computation this course teaches. The execution rationale erodes and F1 rises. But construction materials are placed on physical sites under variable conditions, and the embodied judgment to sample correctly, evaluate a pour, and verify that automated results are trustworthy before structures are built stays a human competence; embodiment does not disappear by 2036. The deterministic rule lifts the rating only to Medium, held down by the field-and-verification core. Ten-year uncertainty is wide; I hedge on how far materials QC autonomizes versus remaining human-supervised for structural-safety liability. The honest read: mix design and test analysis automate, yet the embodied, failure-critical materials-and-placement work resists direct substitution, so instrumental necessity erodes only partway. Rating Medium.
CPM 3040.d: Students in this course are introduced to the fundamentals of soils and concrete in construction management, focusing on classification, testing, mix design, placement, and quality control. Emphasis is on practical applications for site evaluation, safety, and construction practices.

r: Project Delivery and Scheduling teaches construction delivery methods and scheduling — comparing traditional and alternative delivery, understanding execution roles, and developing schedules in industry software, including baseline schedules, Critical Path Method networks, and managing updates, reviews, and change orders. The applied work is squarely analytical PM: building and manipulating CPM networks, optimizing sequences, and processing schedule changes, mapping to O*NET's scheduling-work, organizing-planning, and analyzing-data activities. Scheduling is highly automatable — observed-usage data places computational and management tasks among the largest usage shares — and software already computes critical paths, with AI adding generative scheduling and change-order analysis. There is no embodiment barrier and no licensure lock; the binding constraint is exposure. At 24 months, near-zero curricular change and partial adoption (Census puts firm use near a fifth) keep realized substitution incomplete, and the course's role feeding the capstone provides a mild floor. Rating Medium — exposed scheduling knowledge, not yet fully displaced.

By 2031, AI will generate, optimize, and update construction schedules with facility — building CPM networks from scope, sequencing under constraints, and analyzing change-order impacts — the core applied tasks this course teaches. Task-exposure research and observed usage both place computational planning among the most exposed activities, and no embodiment, licensure, or foundational cap binds. The residual is judgment about delivery-method selection and stakeholder-driven schedule realism, real but narrower than the scheduling mechanics that dominate the course. The rating rises to High. The hedge is verification-flavored: an AI-generated schedule can be confidently unrealistic, and the jagged-frontier evidence shows users misjudging such output, so a knowledgeable planner who catches it retains value. But that oversight competence is a fraction of the course's content, and the bulk — CPM construction, updating, change management — is squarely automatable. Rating High, with instrumental necessity shifting from producing schedules to validating them.

A decade out, AI will produce and manage construction schedules end-to-end — generative sequencing, continuous updating from field data, automated change-order analysis — and the scheduling knowledge-work this course teaches is largely performed by machines. The instrumental case for learning to build CPM networks by hand is substantially eroded, with practitioners concentrated in delivery strategy and validation. No structural constraint holds the rating down. Rating High. The ten-year band is wide; I hedge on diffusion, since construction is fragmented and field-anchored and adoption may trail capability, and on the durable residue of human judgment about which schedule is realistic under real jobsite conditions. The honest framing: the analytical scheduling core automates substantially, and the course's instrumental necessity erodes markedly, even as someone must still own the schedule's consequences. The most persistent competence is catching the plausible-but-wrong plan, which this course only partly emphasizes. Rating High.
CPM 3120.d: Students in this course gain a foundational understanding of construction project delivery methods and project scheduling. Emphasis is placed on comparing traditional and alternative delivery methods, understanding roles and responsibilities in project execution, and developing project schedules using industry software. Students create baseline schedules, analyze Critical Path Method (CPM) networks, and manage schedule updates, reviews, and change orders.

r: Construction Documents introduces the documents used on construction projects, their hierarchy and relationships, how they support execution, and applying technology platforms to manage documentation and submissions, emphasizing document control, quality, and compliance. The applied work is document processing and administrative control — organizing submittals, tracking RFIs, and managing compliance records — mapping to O*NET's documenting/recording, processing-information, and organizing activities. This is digital administrative knowledge-work with no embodiment barrier; observed-usage data shows office and information tasks are prominent in model use, and AI already drafts, classifies, and routes construction documents. There is no licensure lock. At 24 months, the constraint is diffusion and the course's role feeding CPM 4000: near-zero curricular change and partial firm adoption keep realized substitution incomplete. Rating Medium — document-control knowledge is highly exposed, but the near-term erosion is partial rather than complete.

By 2031, AI will perform much of the construction-document control this course teaches — organizing and cross-referencing document hierarchies, processing submittals and RFIs, and flagging compliance gaps — squarely in the office-and-information tasks observed usage shows models handle prominently. Enterprise deployment skews toward automating exactly this kind of administrative document work. With no embodiment, no licensure mandate, and only a contributory role in the sequence, little caps the rating. The residual is judgment about contractual document relationships and dispute-relevant compliance, narrower than the control-and-processing bulk. The rating rises to High. The hedge is that construction documentation is contractually consequential and error-sensitive, so a verification role persists — an AI misfiling or misreading a submittal has real liability implications, per the jagged-frontier caution. But that oversight is a fraction of the course, and the document-management core is broadly automatable. Rating High, with necessity shifting toward validation.

A decade out, AI will handle construction document control end-to-end — automated submittal and RFI processing, continuous compliance checking, and integrated document platforms — performing the administrative knowledge-work this course teaches. The instrumental case for learning to manage document hierarchies by hand is substantially eroded, with humans focused on contractual judgment and dispute-relevant verification. No structural constraint holds the rating down. Rating High. The ten-year band is wide; I hedge on diffusion, since construction's fragmented delivery and contractual conservatism may slow adoption below the capability frontier, and on the durable premium for humans who can verify that an automated document system has not created a costly contractual error. The honest framing: the document-processing core automates substantially and the course's instrumental necessity erodes markedly, even as accountability for the contract record stays human. The most persistent competence is catching the consequential misfile, which the course only partly emphasizes. Rating High.
CPM 3300.d: Students in this course are introduced to the construction documents commonly used in construction projects. Students explore the hierarchy and relationships among these documents, learn how they support project execution, and apply technology platforms to manage documentation and submissions. Emphasis is placed on document control, quality, and compliance with industry standards.
